about.label: About the park
about.heading: Where the Mekong meets 200 statues
about.lead: Buddha Park (Wat Xieng Khouane Luang) is a sculptural garden on the eastern bank of the Mekong, just outside Vientiane — a quiet, otherworldly place where Buddhism and Hinduism share the same lawn.
about.paragraph1: The park was founded in 1958 by Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat, a mystic priest who studied both Buddhist and Hindu teaching. He gathered local craftsmen to mould more than 200 statues in reinforced concrete, blending the two faiths into one riverside garden.
about.paragraph2: Today Buddha Park is one of Vientiane's most surreal stops. Wandering between a 40-metre reclining Buddha, a giant pumpkin you climb from Hell to Heaven, and a three-headed elephant is unlike anywhere else in Laos.
about.quote: Walk slowly — the park reveals itself one statue at a time.

history.label: History
history.heading: From a monk's vision to a riverside park
history.intro: The story of Buddha Park is the story of one man's unusual faith — built in concrete on the banks of the Mekong.

blocks.title: Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat
blocks.text: In 1958 the mystic figure Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat founded the park. No ordinary monk, he was a shamanic recluse who blended Hinduism and Buddhism — legend says that as a young man he fell into a cave and was tutored by a Hindu hermit, setting him on a spiritual path outside orthodox religion, fusing the two faiths into one riverside garden.

blocks.title: A garden of two faiths
blocks.text: Over the following years more than 200 figures were cast in concrete — Buddhas, Avalokiteshvara, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Rama and Hanuman sharing the same lawns.

blocks.title: Today
blocks.text: After decades the park remains a relaxed, slightly surreal stop on Vientiane's eastern edge, drawing travellers who cross the river from Thailand's Nong Khai.

blocks.title: A sister park across the river
blocks.text: In 1975, as Laos came under communist rule, Bunleua Sulilat crossed the Mekong to Thailand. In Nong Khai he built Sala Keoku — a sibling sculpture park born of the same vision. One river, two banks, two parks shaped by the same hand.

legend.title: The meaning of 'Xieng Khouane'
legend.text: Locals call it Wat Xieng Khouane. In Lao, Xieng means 'sacred city / city' and Khouane means 'soul / spirit', so the full name translates as 'City of Spirits'. It marks the park's identity as a 'city of statues' while hinting at the animist folk beliefs woven through it.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: The giant Pumpkin Tower (also the 'Three Realms Tower') is a three-storey sphere that mirrors the Buddhist cosmology of the 'Three Realms (Traiphum)': enter through a demon's mouth, climb narrow steps in the dark through Hell and the human world, and finally emerge into light at the top — overlooking the whole spirit-city by the Mekong, a symbol of transcending the cycle of rebirth.

folklore.title: A place of spirits
folklore.tale: In Lao folk belief the Mekong is home to spirits (Phi). Small shrines near the water ask for safety and luck — a quiet tradition elders still remember.
folklore.shrine: If you see a small shrine or offerings by the water, admire from a distance and do not disturb them.

concrete.title: Concrete Brutalist Aesthetics
concrete.text: These colossal figures were not finely carved in marble but cast on-site in industrial reinforced concrete. The raw textures and exaggerated proportions express a mid-20th-century Lao folk-art brutalism that is rough yet full of vitality — giving Buddha Park its one-of-a-kind surreal landscape.

sisterQuote.title: A mystic fate across one river
sisterQuote.text: In 1975 Luang Pu crossed the Mekong to Nong Khai, Thailand, and built the sister park Sala Keoku. One master, two parks, facing each other across the river.

items.title: From Vientiane
items.desc: About 25 km east of the centre; tuk-tuk or bus toward the Thai–Lao Friendship Bridge.

items.title: Local bus
items.desc: Public buses run from the capital's bus stations to the Deua / Friendship Bridge road.

items.title: From Nong Khai, Thailand
items.desc: Cross the river by the Friendship Bridge, then continue to the park on the Lao side.

items.title: Bus No. 14
items.desc: From Talat Sao Bus Terminal in Vientiane, take Bus No. 14 — its final stop is Buddha Park. Fare is about 6,000 LAK, the cheapest and most classic public transport for backpackers.

items.title: From Wattay International Airport (VTE)
items.desc: Wattay International Airport is about 30 km from the park. Take an airport taxi or a ride-hailing app to the city or the park (around 40–60 min), or save money by heading to Talat Sao first and catching Bus No. 14.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Buddha Park?
faqs.a: The park is open daily about 08:00–17:00. Mornings are coolest and quietest.
Yes — about 15,000 LAK for foreign visitors, plus around 5,000 LAK if you bring a camera.

faqs.q: How do I get there from Vientiane?
faqs.a: It's about 25 km east of the centre; take a tuk-tuk or public bus toward the Friendship Bridge.

faqs.q: Is the giant pumpkin worth climbing?
faqs.a: Yes — the three-storey sphere climbs from Hell to Heaven, with a rooftop view over the Mekong.
Very — flat lawns, a riverside walk and the playful statues, but watch children on the narrow pumpkin stairs.
